vignette:
James is nineteen years old and works at a fast-food restaurant in a bustling suburban area. He has been employed there for just over a year, flipping burgers and taking orders, while dreaming of a future in environmental science. As a child, he would often gaze at the sky, fascinated by the changing weather patterns. But on one fateful day, that fascination turned into deep-rooted fear.

It was a sunny afternoon in early spring when James, along with his friends, decided to take advantage of the pleasant weather and go hiking at a nearby nature reserve. They had trekked this path many times before, enjoying the thrill of nature’s beauty and camaraderie. But that day, dark clouds rolled in unexpectedly, and the winds picked up. Within moments, a severe thunderstorm swept through the area, catching everyone off guard. The group sought refuge under a large oak tree, thinking it would provide shelter. But the storm escalated quickly, and in a matter of minutes, a massive, uprooted tree crashed down, striking James and his friend Alex, who stood too close.

James remembers the deafening sound of the tree splitting the air, the shouts of his friends, and then silence. The world around him blurred; he could feel his heart racing, and an overwhelming sense of dread seized him. He was conscious of the chaos, of blood on the ground, of Alex's stillness. He remembers screaming for help, desperately trying to shake Alex awake, but the panic coursing through his body rendered him helpless. It wasn’t until later that the paramedics arrived that he understood the gravity of the situation.

Since that day, everything has changed for James. He feels as if he is living in a fog, one that is dense and suffocating. At work, the sizzling of the grill and the chatter of customers feel overwhelming. The fast-paced environment, once a source of comfort, now triggers memories of the storm. He finds himself zoning out during shifts, plagued by intrusive thoughts that bring him back to that moment under the tree. Sometimes, the smell of rain wafts through the restaurant, and his heart races as he feels the first drops fall. He can’t escape the images of Alex’s lifeless body.

At home, James struggles to find solace. On some nights, he lays awake, the shadows in his room morphing into reminders of the disaster. He avoids looking at the news, fearing reports of bad weather or natural disasters that could trigger memories he is trying to escape. He has withdrawn from his friends, feeling like a ghost in his own life. When they reach out, he often responds with short, disinterested texts, too exhausted to share his truth. The laughter they once shared feels like a distant echo, a reminder of a happiness he no longer believes he can reclaim.

When he does venture out, he finds himself constantly scanning his environment, hyper-aware of every sound and movement. The world feels unpredictable, just like that day in the woods. He is often irritable, snapping at his coworkers over trivial issues, which only adds to his isolation. They don't understand why he seems so distant, why he flinches at sudden noises or why he storms out during a rain shower. He knows he should explain, but the words are stuck in his throat.

One evening, after a particularly taxing shift where the storm outside matched the turmoil inside him, James finds himself sitting in his car in the dark parking lot. He grips the steering wheel tightly, his knuckles white. With tears streaming down his face, he feels the weight of his grief and guilt. Why did he survive when Alex did not? The question haunts him relentlessly, a thought that spirals into self-blame and despair. 

As he drives home, the familiar streets feel foreign, like a dream he can’t escape. The world outside continues to move forward while he feels trapped in the past, longing for a return to the boy who loved the rain and the sky. But now, every drop that falls feels like a reminder of what he lost, and every thunderclap is a battle cry of his unresolved anguish. James navigates his days in a haze, searching for a way to reconcile the joyful memories of his youth with the heavy shadows of his trauma. He knows he can’t keep living like this forever, but he feels lost, unsure of where to turn next.
